titre: A positive test on a deck of cards, sixteen years in prison
accroche: England, 1974: an expert says he is 99% sure two men handled explosives. The same test also reacts to playing cards.
contenu_vulgarise:
On November 21, 1974, two bombs explode in Birmingham pubs: 21 dead, at least 170 injured. Six men are arrested and interrogated, and four of them sign confessions, which they later attribute to violence suffered in custody. At trial, a scientific element supports the disputed confessions: Home Office scientist Frank Skuse had subjected the hands of two of the accused, Patrick Hill and William Power, to the Griess test, which reveals the presence of nitrites by a red coloring. He says he is 99% sure that the two men had handled explosives. The trial judge, Mr Justice Bridge, accepts his conclusion over that of a defense expert, Dr. Hugh Black, who disputes it. The six men are sentenced to life in 1975.

## What the test could not tell apart

The Griess test detects nitrite ions, which caustic soda brings out of nitroglycerine. But it also reacts to other substances: laboratory detergents, certain soaps and varnishes, or the nitrocellulose that playing cards were once coated with. A positive result alone therefore cannot tell a man who handled an explosive from a man who simply played cards. Yet the five men arrested at Heysham had played cards on the train. Chris Mullin, the journalist who investigated the case, points out that the Griess test is only a screening test: Skuse should have brought the samples back to his laboratory to run them through a mass spectrometer, far more precise. He told the police he was certain, then, on the stand, “99% sure.”

## Sixteen years before the quashing

Arrested in November 1974 and convicted in 1975, the six men see their case referred to the Court of Appeal by the Home Secretary, Douglas Hurd. After a six-week hearing, the court in January 1988 finds the convictions safe and satisfactory. In the meantime, Mullin investigates for the program *World in Action*: a first broadcast casts doubt in 1985, and his book *Error of Judgment* appears in 1986. The team has one of its own, Ian McBride, shuffle an old deck of cards: his hands give a positive Griess test, like the accused's in 1974. Later analyses, by gas chromatography coupled with mass spectrometry, come back negative for William Power and contradict the original result for Patrick Hill.

## What the Court of Appeal says

On March 14, 1991, the Court of Appeal quashes the six convictions, which it finds “unsafe and unsatisfactory.” The new scientific evidence casts serious doubt on Skuse's testimony: according to the court, his conclusion was wrong, and demonstrably wrong, even by the state of forensic science in 1974, and the Griess test should serve only as a preliminary test. The six men, including Hugh Callaghan and John Walker, are released the same day, more than sixteen years after their arrest.

## The shift

A Royal Commission on Criminal Justice is set up in 1991; its recommendations lead to the Criminal Appeal Act of 1995, which creates in 1997 the Criminal Cases Review Commission, tasked with referring to the courts cases it finds doubtful. The Griess test itself is not at fault: it is a filter, designed to be followed by other analyses. What the case shows is what happens when a screening result arrives in court with the assurance of certainty: 99%, pronounced without the reservation the method itself imposed.

repere.texte: On March 14, 1991, the Court of Appeal of England and Wales quashes the six life sentences handed down in 1975 against the “Birmingham Six,” finding them “unsafe and unsatisfactory.”
repere.source: Criminal Cases Review Commission, anniversary of the quashed convictions

carte.punch: The test that came back positive for explosives also reacted to playing cards
carte.idee: In 1974, an expert says he is 99% sure two men handled explosives, based on a test that also reacts to ordinary substances. Sixteen years later, in 1991, the six convictions, resting on disputed confessions and this test, are quashed.
carte.source_courte: Criminal Cases Review Commission, United Kingdom

quiz.question: Why did the Griess test result, presented as 99% reliable in 1974, prove misleading in the Birmingham Six case?
choix: Because the expert had swapped the samples of two different defendants before analyzing them
Because the test also reacts to ordinary substances, such as the nitrocellulose on playing cards
Because the test detects only military explosives, not those used by bombers
Because the Home Office laboratory did not yet have the equipment needed to run it properly
quiz.explication: The Griess test detects nitrites, which nitroglycerine produces but which common substances also give, such as the nitrocellulose that playing cards were coated with. A journalist who shuffled an old deck of cards got a positive test, like the hands of two defendants in 1974: the test alone could not settle the question.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How much time passes between the conviction of the Birmingham Six and the quashing of their convictions?
choix: About six years, the time of a single appeal brought directly before the Court of Appeal
About sixteen years, including an appeal rejected in January 1988 after a six-week hearing
About thirty years, the case having been reopened only after the CCRC was created in 1997
About two years, the court having quickly recognized the weakness of the Griess test used in 1974
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Convicted in 1975, the six men see their case referred to the Court of Appeal, which rejects the appeals in January 1988 after a six-week hearing. The same court quashes the convictions on March 14, 1991: sixteen years after the conviction.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the Court of Appeal say in 1991 about the conclusion given by expert Frank Skuse in 1974?
choix: That it remained broadly valid, even if the sentence handed down deserved to be reduced
That it was wrong, and demonstrably wrong, even by the science of the time
That it had never been put to the jury, which had ruled on the defendants' confessions alone
That it came from an unaccredited laboratory, unconnected with Home Office methods
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The Court of Appeal does not merely doubt: it finds Skuse's conclusion wrong, and demonstrably wrong, even by the state of forensic science in 1974, and holds that the Griess test should serve only as a preliminary test.
